title: Cost Ops + Quantization & Batching Discovery - Lambda Finance
summary: Exploratory discovery focused on per-token economics and architecture choices (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer is cost-sensitive with strict latency SLAs for pricing quote generator and compliance screen; interested in quantization and caching levers, pilot metrics, and proof points for predictable unit cost at scale.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-10
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO, Lambda Finance), Maya Chen (Head of ML), Rafael Ortiz (Infra Lead)

[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'll kick off, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. Quick check, Jordan, do you want to say hi and confirm the agenda?

[00:00:18] Jordan: Yep, hi all. Jordan here. We're mostly focused on understanding what our unit economics would look like for a pricing generator and a realtime compliance screen that runs alongside. We have some hard budget constraints and low latency needs.

[00:00:35] Priya: Great, thanks. Today we planned to walk through how Redwood approaches per-token pricing across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, batching and caching levers, and quantization tradeoffs. Also capture workload details so we can propose a pilot.

[00:00:50] Maya: Quick note — our SLA for the pricing generator is 200 ms p95 for 95% of requests; compliance screen can tolerate up to 600 ms p95 but needs deterministic behavior.

[00:01:05] Rafael: And infra-wise we can't send sensitive transaction payloads to third-party unless encrypted in transit with customer KMS and there's audit logs. So security is big.

[00:01:22] Alex: Totally understood. We'll cover security briefly and include SOC2/KMS notes in the follow-up. Before we dig in, Justin from procurement wanted to flag a 6-week procurement window — not urgent but part of the timeline.

[00:01:38] Jordan: Sounds good. Let's go into cost. How does Redwood price per token across the modes?

[00:01:45] Priya: Short answer: hosted is usage-based per-token with model-dependent multipliers, dedicated is a reserved capacity contract (CPU/GPU pool) with predictable throughput and lower per-token at scale, private has platform fees and depends on your infra cost — we can help model that. Important levers are batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization which materially reduce tokens billed or GPU cycles.

[00:02:10] Maya: Can you quantify — if we push to int8 quant (or q4) what difference do we see? Also how batch size impacts latency vs cost — we need to preserve that 200 ms p95.

[00:02:26] Priya: From our benchmark set, going from FP16 to 8-bit quantization usually reduces GPU memory and increases throughput 1.8x–3x depending on model and kernel support; cost per token often drops ~25–45% but quality delta varies. For small prompts with short contexts, batching helps but you hit latency cliff — continuous batching with small max-wait thresholds can help.

[00:02:52] Jordan: When you say batching helps, is that on the Redwood side or do we have to change our client to batch requests?

[00:03:00] Priya: Redwood runtime can perform server-side batching automatically within a configured window. You can also do client-side batching if you want more control. We typically suggest a hybrid: enable server batching with a max-wait of 20–30ms for low-latency SMBs, and allow client grouping for bulk jobs.

[00:03:18] Rafael: Our traffic profile is spiky during market opens, bursts up 10x. How does reserved capacity handle that? Any burst options?

[00:03:28] Alex: Dedicated pools can be configured with burst capacity to handle spikes; you reserve baseline and set burst budget for temporary capacity usage that incurs overage. We can simulate your spike profile in the pilot to size the pool.

[00:03:43] Maya: Ok, let's talk about caching. We have a lot of repeated prefixes for pricing tables and standard legal boilerplate. Can that reduce token count billed?

[00:03:55] Priya: Yes — KV cache / prefix caching avoids regenerating identical prefixes. There are two effects: reduces compute tokens and reduces end-to-end latency. Billing depends — some customers use token-level billing but we apply caching-aware suggestions; in dedicated deployments you can also implement warm-start KVs persisted across requests. Note, some transcripts call it "KV cash" in older docs — that's a transcription quirk, but we mean cache.

[00:04:20] Jordan: Is there any billing model where cached tokens aren't charged?

[00:04:27] Priya: In hosted mode we bill per output token; cached prefixes mean fewer output tokens to generate. For private/dedicated where you buy reserved capacity, you effectively amortize cost over capacity so cache improves throughput and reduces GPU-hours per effective token. We can show you a modeled example with your prompt distribution.

[00:04:43] Maya: We run some long contexts — up to 4k tokens — will that break batching or quantization benefits?

[00:04:50] Priya: Larger contexts increase memory pressure but our runtime selects kernels and execution paths optimized for sequence length. For 4k, certain quant kernels perform better; we will recommend model variants and chunking strategies. Batching becomes trickier because memory limits reduce batch size; that's where dedicated with higher-memory GPUs helps.

[00:05:12] Jordan: Can you give an example TCO? Say 100k inference requests/day, average 300 tokens output, 50k of those reuse cached prefixes. What's the monthly bill hosted vs dedicated?

[00:05:26] Alex: We didn't run your exact numbers in the call yet, but rough back-of-envelope: hosted per-token on a medium Llama-type model might be $0.000012/token (example number), so 100k * 300 = 30M tokens => ~$360/month before caching. If 50k requests reuse 100 tokens each, that's 5M cached tokens not generated => roughly $300 difference. Dedicated with a reserved pool might cost $X/month but result in per-token equivalent of $0.000007–0.000009 depending on utilization. We'll send a spreadsheet with scenarios.

[00:06:01] Rafael: That example per-token number seems low — is that for inference only or includes support/console charges?

[00:06:09] Alex: Hosted includes inference + basic platform usage. Dedicated has a platform fee plus reserved capacity. We'll itemize in the model.

[00:06:18] Maya: You mentioned model variants — are you recommending we run smaller tuned models for pricing and a larger model for compliance?

[00:06:26] Priya: Exactly. Multi-tier routing is a common pattern: cheap tuned model for pricing generation latency-critical paths, and fallback to a larger model for complex cases or when quality thresholds aren't met. Redwood supports policy-based routing so you can set deterministic fallbacks.

[00:06:40] Jordan: How do you measure quality regressions if we quantize? We can't have pricing errors.

[00:06:48] Priya: We recommend a gating eval set — sample of your critical prompts. Redwood Optimize can run A/B with metrics (token-level diff, business-specific checks). We'll include suggested test prompts and thresholds to validate quant profiles before rollout.

[00:07:05] Maya: For the compliance screen, deterministic output and audit logs are key. Are logs stored in Redwood? Can we send logs to our SIEM?

[00:07:13] Alex: Logs can be retained in Redwood with configurable retention or shipped via secure syslog/S3 to your account and integrated with your SIEM. For private deployments, logs remain in your VPC by default. KMS integration for encryption at rest is supported.

[00:07:28] Rafael: Any differences in latency SLAs across modes?

[00:07:33] Priya: Hosted has public SLOs and typical p95 numbers for each model. Dedicated gets guaranteed latency bands tied to your reserved pool and SLA. Private depends on your infra but Redwood will provide guidance.

[00:07:45] Jordan: Let's talk pilot. We want a pilot that gives us real unit economics. What would Redwood propose?

[00:07:53] Priya: We propose a 4-week pilot: week 0–1 integrate telemetry and run a small traffic replay (you said you'd share traces), week 2 run micro-benchmarks with targeted quant profiles and batching windows, week 3 run a small production shadow test for the pricing generator routing 5–10% of traffic, week 4 analyze cost/latency and produce a recommended config. We'll include a cost model exported as CSV.

[00:08:22] Jordan: Can you simulate peak bursts so we understand burst costs?

[00:08:27] Alex: Yes, we'll replay traffic and run spike simulations; for hosted we'll show cost under current pricing and for dedicated we'll show reserved + burst overage scenarios.

[00:08:36] Rafael: Any procurement constraints for a pilot? We might need a short statement of work or PO.

[00:08:41] Alex: We can do a pilot agreement or an evaluation addendum — standard practice for enterprise pilots. We'll send a templated SOW.

[00:08:48] Maya: On security would you share SOC2 and the KMS integration guide? Also a diagram for private deployment options?

[00:08:55] Alex: Yes — action item: include SOC2, KMS guide, private deployment diagram, and a sample SLA.

[00:09:02] Jordan: Who will be our contacts for the pilot?

[00:09:06] Priya: Priya will own technical delivery; Alex on commercial; Rafael can loop in three infra folks directly if needed.

[00:09:14] [00:09:30] Guilding the technical: Priya: A few more technical clarifications — what GPU inventory or on-prem footprint would you prefer if you consider private?

[00:09:37] Rafael: Ideally not on-prem to start; if private, we'd likely evaluate GCP VMs with A100s or private tenancy with A10G for cost control.

[00:09:49] Priya: For A100 you get better large-context perf; A10Gs are cost-effective for smaller models. We'll include that in the TCO comparison.

[00:09:58] Jordan: Are there any caveats around quantization and long context windows?

[00:10:03] Priya: Some quant kernels don't support very long KV caches efficiently; you'll see more benefit from dedicated setups with larger memory or model partitioning. We'll flag recommended quantization levels per-model/context.

[00:10:16] Maya: How do we handle model updates and rollouts? We need canarying and quick rollback.

[00:10:21] Alex: Redwood Console has rollout tools: canary, A/B, automatic fallback based on quality regressions or latency breaches. Rollback is instantaneous to pinned version.

[00:10:31] Jordan: Ok that's helpful. I want to capture an example cost scenario in the spreadsheet for our CFO — can you include a conservative, expected, and aggressive utilization scenario?

[00:10:40] Alex: Yes, we will. We'll add utilization bands and show effective per-token cost under each.

[00:10:46] Rafael: Regarding caching, does the runtime persist KVs across restarts so warm start is possible?

[00:10:53] Priya: For dedicated/private you can configure persistent KV stores to survive restarts; hosted has warm caches but persistence is limited — we'll outline exact semantics.

[00:11:05] Maya: Any concerns about vendor lock-in if we start with Redwood hosted and later move to private?

[00:11:12] Alex: We designed the API and models to be portable; deployments are consistent across modes so migration is straightforward. We'll show a migration playbook.

[00:11:21] Jordan: What's the cost delta moving from hosted to dedicated typically? At what point does dedicated pay off?

[00:11:27] Priya: Depends on utilization. If you're >30–40% utilization of a reserved pool, dedicated often yields lower effective cost, especially with heavy caching and batching. We'll calculate exact breakeven in the spreadsheet for your traffic.

[00:11:39] [00:11:50] Some cross talk — inaudible for a second

[00:11:57] Priya: One more question on output token lengths — do you have a long tail of very large responses?

[00:12:03] Maya: Yes, 2% of responses are >1k tokens, the rest are sub-400 tokens.

[00:12:10] Priya: Good to know — that tail will push up memory and reduce effective batch sizes. We will include a hybrid model: route short responses to aggressive batching/quant profiles and long tails to larger instances or dynamic routing.

[00:12:27] Jordan: Sounds reasonable. Anything else on infra?

[00:12:31] Rafael: If we go dedicated will we manage autoscaling policies? We want to set max-cost caps.

[00:12:37] Alex: Yes — Redwood lets you set autoscale knobs and cost caps; you can also set fallback rules to lower-cost model variants if budget thresholds are approaching.

[00:12:47] Maya: We need to confirm the legal/compliance review items — any special certifications beyond SOC2 we should expect?

[00:12:54] Alex: SOC2 is primary; ISO/27001 we're working on and can share roadmap. For regulated data flows we recommend private with customer-managed KMS.

[00:13:06] Jordan: Ok let's capture the explicit next steps and owners.

[00:13:11] Alex: I'll recap. Action items — send spreadsheet, SOW template, SOC2/KMS docs, run micro-benchmark plan. Priya will draft pilot plan and recommended quant configs. Maya will share traces. Rafael will confirm which cloud and any network egress constraints.

[00:13:29] Maya: We'll try to get those artifacts by EOD Monday.

[00:13:33] Alex: Great. Any final questions?

[00:13:37] Jordan: One last — do you have an example where caching reduced costs 30%+ for a customer?

[00:13:43] Priya: Yes, we have a case study (internal) where cached prefixes reduced generated tokens 40% for a pricing product; we'll include anonymized numbers in the follow-up.

[00:13:54] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll circulate the materials and set the pilot scoping meeting. Meeting ends.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional misheard words (KV cash, bedrock vs bed rock), filler words present, timestamps approximate.
